title: Association versus Causation
student_objective: I can distinguish statistical association from evidence of cause and effect and identify possible lurking variables.

concept_cards.title: Association means variables move together
concept_cards.content: An association means two variables show a pattern together. It does not, by itself, tell us why the pattern occurs.

concept_cards.title: Causation is a stronger claim
concept_cards.content: A causal claim says changing one variable produces a change in another. That requires stronger evidence than correlation alone.

concept_cards.title: Look for lurking variables
concept_cards.content: A third variable can influence both measured variables and create an association that is not direct cause and effect.

concept_cards.title: Study design matters
concept_cards.content: Randomized controlled experiments can support causal conclusions when well designed. Observational data usually support association, not causation, by themselves.

association.teacher_signal: Student treats association as proof of causation.

lurking.teacher_signal: Student overlooks a plausible third variable.

design.teacher_signal: Student ignores how data were collected.

items.prompt: A study finds that students who sleep more tend to earn higher test scores. Does this association alone prove that extra sleep caused the higher scores? Answer yes or no.
items.tutor_behavior: Separate observed association from a causal claim.
hint_steps: The study reports a pattern.
A pattern alone does not establish cause and effect.
No.

solution_steps.explanation: Other differences between students could also matter.

items.prompt: Ice-cream sales and sunburn cases both rise in summer. Which is a plausible lurking variable: temperature, shoe size, or alphabet order?
items.tutor_behavior: Find a third variable that can affect both measured variables.
hint_steps: What changes in summer and could influence both outcomes?
Hotter weather can increase ice-cream purchases and time outdoors.
Temperature is the plausible lurking variable.

solution_steps.equation: higher temperature → more ice cream and more outdoor exposure
solution_steps.explanation: A third variable can help explain both outcomes.

items.prompt: An observational survey finds a strong association between carrying an umbrella and wet sidewalks. Is it reasonable to conclude umbrellas cause wet sidewalks?
items.tutor_behavior: Use rain as the lurking variable.
hint_steps: Ask what causes people to carry umbrellas.
Rain also makes sidewalks wet.
The association does not mean umbrellas cause wet sidewalks.

solution_steps.explanation: Rain increases umbrella use.
Rain also directly wets sidewalks.
Rain explains both variables.

items.prompt: Researchers randomly assign similar plants to two groups. One receives a fertilizer and one does not, while other conditions are controlled. The fertilized group grows more. Which conclusion is better supported: association only or a causal effect of the fertilizer?
items.tutor_behavior: Connect random assignment and control to stronger causal evidence.
hint_steps: The groups were randomly assigned.
Other conditions were controlled.
That design can support a causal effect of the fertilizer.

solution_steps.explanation: The design reduces alternative explanations.
A causal conclusion is better supported.

items.prompt: Neighborhoods with more firefighters at a fire often have greater property damage. Does this mean firefighters cause more damage? Answer yes or no.
items.tutor_behavior: Consider fire severity as a lurking variable.
hint_steps: Larger fires need more firefighters.
Larger fires also tend to cause more damage.
So firefighter count does not by itself cause the damage.

solution_steps.explanation: Severe fires require larger responses.
Severity also raises damage.

items.prompt: A school records that students who attend optional tutoring tend to improve more. The school did not randomly assign tutoring. Should the result be described primarily as association or causation?
items.tutor_behavior: Observational participation can differ in motivation and need.
hint_steps: Students chose whether to attend.
Self-selection can create other differences between groups.
Describe the result as association unless stronger causal evidence is available.

solution_steps.explanation: No random assignment occurred.
The data show a relationship but do not by themselves prove cause.

items.prompt: A city sees a positive correlation between bicycle helmet sales and bicycle injuries during spring. Name one plausible third variable that could affect both.
items.tutor_behavior: Look for exposure that can increase both helmet purchases and injury opportunities.
hint_steps: Think about what changes in spring.
More people may start riding bicycles.
More bicycling can increase both helmet sales and opportunities for injuries.

solution_steps.explanation: More riders may buy helmets.
More riding also creates more opportunities for injury.

items.prompt: A correlation between shoe size and reading ability appears among elementary students. What lurking variable is most plausible?
items.tutor_behavior: Age can increase both shoe size and reading development.
hint_steps: What tends to increase as children get older?
Both shoe size and reading skill can increase with age.
Age is the plausible lurking variable.

solution_steps.equation: age ↑ → shoe size ↑ and reading skill ↑
solution_steps.explanation: Age can affect both variables.

items.prompt: A randomized experiment changes only the amount of light given to otherwise similar plants and finds consistent growth differences. Is a causal conclusion more reasonable than from an observational study? Answer yes or no.
items.tutor_behavior: Use random assignment/control as stronger evidence.
hint_steps: The experiment actively changes light.
Other conditions are controlled.
Yes, this design better supports causation.

solution_steps.explanation: The design directly manipulates the explanatory variable.

items.prompt: If two variables have r=0.96, what can you safely claim from r alone: strong association or proven causation?
items.tutor_behavior: High correlation does not by itself establish causality.
hint_steps: r measures association.
Even r close to 1 is not proof of cause.
Safely claim strong association.

solution_steps.explanation: This indicates strong linear association.
Study design and other evidence are needed for a causal claim.

items.prompt: Two variables are strongly correlated in an observational study. Does that fact alone establish causation?
hint_steps: Correlation measures association.
Observational evidence can have confounding variables.
No.

solution_steps.explanation: Association alone is insufficient for causal proof.

items.prompt: Hot weather is associated with both pool attendance and cold-drink sales. What role can hot weather play?
hint_steps: It can affect both measured variables.
A third variable that influences both is called lurking/confounding.
Hot weather is a lurking variable.

solution_steps.equation: hot weather → pool attendance and drink sales
solution_steps.explanation: It can create the observed association.

items.prompt: Which provides stronger causal evidence: a randomized controlled experiment or an observational correlation?
items.tutor_behavior: Study design determines strength of causal evidence.
hint_steps: Look for active assignment and control.
Random assignment reduces alternative explanations.
The randomized controlled experiment provides stronger causal evidence.

solution_steps.explanation: It better isolates the effect of the treatment.

items.prompt: A study reports that people who own more books tend to have higher vocabulary scores. Give one reason not to conclude that buying books automatically causes the score increase.
hint_steps: Think of a third factor tied to both book ownership and vocabulary.
Education, income, or reading habits could affect both.
Other variables may explain part of the association.

solution_steps.explanation: Alternative explanations prevent a simple causal conclusion.

items.prompt: Complete the statement: correlation is evidence of ________, not automatically evidence of ________.
hint_steps: First blank: a statistical relationship.
Second blank: cause and effect.
Association; causation.

solution_steps.explanation: Correlation summarizes a relationship.
A causal conclusion requires stronger evidence.
